items.text: $B_G$ is not a space
For $G\neq 1$, $B_G$ is not equivalent to any $\operatorname{Top}(X)$.
\varphi\colon B_G\to\mathbf{Sets}\quad\text{forgetful functor}
A fibre functor: commutes with all limits (computed set-theoretically).
\operatorname{Aut}(\varphi)\simeq G
Fibre functors on $\operatorname{Top}(X)$ have no non-trivial automorphisms. Digression: homomorphisms between fibre functors.
Specialisation
$X$ sober (replacing $X$ does not change $\operatorname{Top}(X)$ up to equivalence); every fibre functor is $F\mapsto F_x$.
y\ \text{is a specialisation of}\ x\iff y\in\overline{\{x\}}
A pre-order; an order if $X$ is sober.
F_y=\varinjlim_{U\ni y}F(U)\ \longrightarrow\ \varinjlim_{V\ni x}F(V)=F_x
Every neighbourhood of $y$ contains $x$: the neighbourhoods of $y$ are among those of $x$. Functorial in $F$.
The category $\operatorname{Cat}(X)$ of the ordered set $X$:
\operatorname{Hom}(y,x)=\begin{cases}\{*\}&y\ \text{specialisation of}\ x\\ \varnothing&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}
x\mapsto\varepsilon_x\colon\ \operatorname{Cat}(X)^{\circ}\to\{\text{fibre functors on }\operatorname{Top}(X)\}
\operatorname{Hom}(\varepsilon_y,\varepsilon_x)\neq\varnothing\iff y\in\overline{\{x\}},\ \text{and then it has one element}
In particular no non-trivial automorphisms.
For $B_G$: essentially one fibre functor, with automorphism group $G$ — one point, but not the final topos.
Points of a topos can have automorphisms and homomorphisms; so can continuous maps.
Fibre functors on $\operatorname{Top}(X,G)$
\varepsilon_x^{G}\colon\ \operatorname{Top}(X,G)\to\operatorname{Top}(X)\xrightarrow{\ F\mapsto F_x\ }\mathbf{Sets}
\operatorname{Aut}(\varepsilon_x^G)\simeq G_x=\{g\in G:\ gx=x\}\quad\text{(isotropy group)}
Isotropy groups = automorphism groups of points of the topos.
More on the definition of a topos
Equivalent form: a small category $C$ and a fully faithful $E\hookrightarrow\hat C$ with a left exact left adjoint.
f_*\colon E\hookrightarrow\hat C,\qquad f^*\dashv f_*,\quad f^*\ \text{left exact}
\operatorname{Hom}_E(f^*P,X)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\hat C}(P,f_*X)
As for $\operatorname{Top}(X)\subset\hat{\mathcal O}$ with $a$: this is how exactness properties of $\mathbf{Sets}$ carry over to any topos.
Giraud's theorem gives this. Choice of $C$: any generating full subcategory.
E\to\hat C,\quad X\mapsto\bigl(Z\mapsto\operatorname{Hom}(Z,X)\bigr)_{Z\in C}\quad\text{fully faithful iff } C\ \text{generating}
If $C$ works, any larger one does. A topos is a « direct factor » of some $\hat C$.
Circle: sites $\Rightarrow$ this $\Rightarrow$ (a)-(d) $\Rightarrow$ (Giraud) sheaves on a site. Site not yet defined.
Internal operations
\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(X,Y)\ \text{represents}\ Z\mapsto\operatorname{Hom}_Z(X_Z,Y_Z)=\operatorname{Hom}(X\times Z,Y)
\mathcal P_E\ \text{represents}\ Z\mapsto\operatorname{Sub}(Z)
Key lemma: a contravariant functor $P\colon E^{\circ}\to\mathbf{Sets}$ is representable iff
P\bigl(\varinjlim X_i\bigr)=\varprojlim P(X_i)
True when $E$ has direct limits and a small generating set (SGA 4, exposé I). Both functors above satisfy it.
So the internal operations of sheaves exist in a general topos.
Lawvere–Tierney
Different axioms: finite inverse limits, $\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}$ and $\mathcal P_E$ representable.
Probably in between: finite versions only; no generators. Advantage: the axioms are finitary (products, final object, kernels).
$\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}$ is a very strong operation; effectiveness of equivalence relations is then provable.
More examples
$\operatorname{Top}(X,G)$: limits as in $\operatorname{Top}(X)$ with $G$-action; $\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}$ and $\mathcal P_X$ inherit the action.
Presheaf topoi
$C$ a small category; $\hat C$ = contravariant functors $C\to\mathbf{Sets}$.
\bigl(\varinjlim F_i\bigr)(Z)=\varinjlim F_i(Z),\qquad \bigl(\varprojlim F_i\bigr)(Z)=\varprojlim F_i(Z)
All exactness properties of $\mathbf{Sets}$ hold — even with infinite inverse limits. $C$ generates.
A topos sharing all exactness properties of sets is of this type.
$C$ with one object and endomorphisms $G$:
\hat C=B_G
F\mapsto F(X)\quad X\in C:\ \text{fibre functor, commutes with all limits}
Adding filtering direct limits of those gives all fibre functors. Enough points.
Classifying topos of a topological group
Groups in a topos: a topological group is a group object in topological spaces, which embed in a topos (later, with sites).
$E$ a topos, $G$ a group object of $E$:
B_G=\{X\in E\ \text{with an action}\ G\times X\to X\}
(a), (b), (c) carry over. $E=\mathbf{Sets}$ gives back the classifying topos of a discrete group.
Abelian objects of $B_G$: abelian objects of $E$ with $G$ acting by automorphisms.
H^i(G,M)=H^i(B_G,M)
\Gamma(X)=\operatorname{Hom}_{B_G}(e,X)=\Gamma(E,X)^{G}\quad(\text{invariant sections})
Sections of the subsheaf of $G$-invariants of $X$. Left exact; derive on abelian objects.
Justifies the name: $B_G$ classifies torsors under $G$ (exercise).
Needs morphisms of topoi first: postponed.
Induced topos
X\in E:\qquad E/X=\{\text{objects of } E \text{ over } X\}\ \text{a topos}
\operatorname{Top}(Y)/X\simeq\operatorname{Top}(X)\qquad X\ \text{étale over } Y
Identify the object $X$ with its induced topos $E/X$.
Objects of a topos = étale spaces over the (generalised) space; the induced topos over an object is the object itself.
Strictly speaking not legitimate, but statements justify the abuse.
Morphisms of topoi
Almost more important than the definition of a topos. Write « continuous map ».
$E=\operatorname{Top}(X)$, $F=\operatorname{Top}(Y)$ sober: maps $X\to Y$ should be functors back:
f^*\colon F\to E\quad\text{commuting with direct limits and finite inverse limits}
Internal logic of exactness vs. logic from spaces as models.
Direct limits $\Rightarrow$ a right adjoint $f_*\colon E\to F$.
\operatorname{Hom}_F\bigl(Y',f_*X'\bigr)=\operatorname{Hom}_E\bigl(f^*Y',X'\bigr)
Existence of $f_*$ needs only that $f^*$ commutes with direct limits: represent $Y'\mapsto\operatorname{Hom}_E(f^*Y',X')$.
